Although such weak dynamical tidal signatures are unlikely to be resolved with current detector sensitivities, third generation observations may make them accessible, in which case identifying the weak resonant phase shift would provide information beyond the bulk adiabatic tidal deformability. We build a four class dataset in an eccentric harmonic framework, containing point particle, adiabatic tide, resonant $g$ mode, and pure noise samples, and use Einstein Telescope (ET) and Cosmic Explorer (CE) detector data to test whether this weak resonant phase signature can be identified from noisy time domain strain. The ET, CE, and ET+CE deep learning models reach accuracies of $0.655$, $0.815$, and $0.897$, respectively. On the same simulated samples, the matched filtering method reaches lower accuracies of $0.514$, $0.677$, and $0.689$. This result arises from the fact that the resonant correction manifests as a weak phase morphology difference superimposed on the adiabatic tidal background, whereas matched filtering is sensitive only to the overall similarity. Hence, in the presence of weak phase differences, the neural classifier employed in deep learning is better able to learn these local phase and morphology features from the complete time domain strain segment. The results indicate that joint third generation observations improve the identifiability of weak internal mode phase information.

AI.tldr: This study shows that deep learning applied to simulated third generation gravitational-wave data from eccentric binary neutron star inspirals can better detect weak resonant g mode tidal phase shifts than matched filtering, enabling improved insight into neutron star interior properties with upcoming detectors.
AI.motivation: To probe internal neutron star properties such as stratification, superfluidity, composition gradients, and equation of state via weak dynamical tidal signatures in eccentric binary neutron star systems, which are otherwise challenging to detect with current detectors.
AI.method: Constructed a four-class dataset in an eccentric harmonic framework including point particle, adiabatic tide, resonant g mode, and noise samples; applied deep learning models using ET, CE, and combined ET+CE detector simulated data to identify weak resonant g mode phase signatures from noisy time domain strain; comparison with matched filtering methods was performed.
AI.result: Deep learning models achieved higher classification accuracies (ET: 0.655, CE: 0.815, ET+CE: 0.897) compared to matched filtering (ET: 0.514, CE: 0.677, ET+CE: 0.689), indicating superior sensitivity to weak phase morphology differences characteristic of resonant g mode corrections in tidal signals.
AI.conclusion: Deep learning classifiers, especially when using joint third generation gravitational-wave observations, can more effectively identify weak resonant internal mode phase information than matched filtering methods, suggesting enhanced prospects for probing neutron star internal physics via these weak tidal signatures in future detector data.

title: KiDS-Legacy: Joint analysis of second- and third-order cosmic shear
comment: 14 pages plus appendix, 15 figures, submitted to A&A
summary: Weak lensing by large-scale structure is a powerful cosmological probe. While most analyses rely on second-order correlations, these are primarily sensitive to the parameter combination $S_8 = σ_8 (Ω_m/0.3)^{0.5}$, limiting their ability to constrain $Ω_m$ and other cosmological parameters independently. Higher-order statistics capture non-Gaussian features of the density field and can therefore break parameter degeneracies and extract more cosmological information from weak lensing surveys. We present a joint analysis of second- and third-order cosmic shear in the final data release of the Kilo-Degree Survey (KiDS-Legacy). We combine COSEBIs (Complete Orthogonal Sets of E-/B-mode Integrals) at scales between 2' and 300' with third-order aperture mass moments at scales between 4' and 32' to perform a joint analysis of second- and third-order statistics. Compared to previous KiDS analyses, we implement several methodological advances: an intrinsic alignment model with redshift and mass dependence, a baryon correction model validated on multiple hydrodynamical simulations, and corrections for reduced shear and source clustering. Combining COSEBIs with third-order aperture mass statistics in KiDS-Legacy yields $Ω_m = 0.297^{+0.056}_{-0.040}$ and $S_8 = 0.806^{+0.025}_{-0.023}$, significantly tightening the $Ω_m$ constraints and more than doubling the figure of merit in the $Ω_m$--$S_8$ plane compared to the two-point analysis alone. The third-order measurements pass stringent internal consistency tests, are fully compatible with the KiDS-Legacy 2-point constraints, other 2+3-point lensing results and with Planck CMB measurements within $1σ$, providing no evidence for an $S_8$ tension and demonstrating the maturity of 3-point cosmic shear as a key probe for forthcoming surveys.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that combining second- and third-order weak lensing statistics from KiDS-Legacy enhances cosmological parameter constraints by breaking degeneracies, especially improving Ω_m measurement, with results consistent with Planck CMB data and no evident S_8 tension.
AI.motivation: Second-order weak lensing statistics mainly constrain a combination of cosmological parameters (S_8), limiting independent measurement of Ω_m and other parameters. Higher-order statistics can access non-Gaussian information and break degeneracies, extracting more cosmological information.
AI.method: A joint analysis combining second-order COSEBIs (on scales 2'-300') and third-order aperture mass moments (4'-32') was performed on the KiDS-Legacy survey data. Methodological improvements include models for intrinsic alignment with redshift and mass dependence, baryon corrections validated by simulations, and corrections for reduced shear and source clustering.
AI.result: The combined analysis yields Ω_m = 0.297^{+0.056}_{-0.040} and S_8 = 0.806^{+0.025}_{-0.023}, significantly tightening constraints on Ω_m and more than doubling the figure of merit compared to second-order analysis alone. Third-order measurements pass internal consistency tests and agree with other lensing and Planck CMB constraints within 1σ, showing no S_8 tension.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating third-order cosmic shear statistics alongside second-order measures significantly improves constraints on cosmological parameters, especially Ω_m, and confirms the robustness and maturity of three-point lensing analyses as a complementary cosmological probe for future surveys.

title: Emergent gravity from Michel flow with position dependent adiabatic index
summary: Spherically symmetric, general relativistic Bondi accretion is known as the Michel flow. The stationary integral transonic solutions for the Michel flow has been constructed for multi-component accretion described by an equation of state where the adiabatic index varies with the radial distance along which the streamlines are studied, and the corresponding phase portrait spanned by such radial distance and the flow Mach number has been obtained. Borrowing the techniques used in the dynamical systems theory, the nature of the transonic points of the aforementioned flow has been classified. The steady state flow has been perturbed to study the stability of the stationary solutions, and it has been found that such flows are stable under the (linear) radial perturbation. As a consequence of the stability analysis, the corresponding acoustic space time embedded within the accreting matter has been obtained, and the horizon of the metric of such sonic space time has been identified by constructing the causal structure with the help of the Carter-Penrose diagrams. In this way, the accreting black hole systems in the general relativistic set up has been investigated from various different perspectives - from its astrophysical aspects, from the dynamical systems point of view, as well as within the realm of the classical analogue gravity phenomena.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates general relativistic Bondi accretion with variable adiabatic index, classifies transonic points, proves flow stability under perturbations, and identifies the acoustic horizons, integrating astrophysical and analogue gravity perspectives.
AI.motivation: To analyze the general relativistic Bondi accretion (Michel flow) for multi-component fluids with variable adiabatic index, and to explore the stability and acoustic geometry associated with these flows.
AI.method: Construction of stationary integral transonic solutions, phase portrait analysis for radial distance and Mach number, classification of transonic points using dynamical systems theory, linear radial perturbation analysis for stability, and construction of causal structure via Carter-Penrose diagrams to identify sonic horizons.
AI.result: Stationary transonic solutions were found to be stable under linear radial perturbations; the corresponding acoustic spacetime and its horizon were identified and characterized, linking accreting black hole systems to classical analogue gravity phenomena.
AI.conclusion: The study provides a comprehensive analysis of relativistic accretion flows with variable adiabatic index, demonstrating their stability and uncovering the sonic horizon structure within the accreting matter, thus bridging astrophysical, dynamical systems, and analogue gravity frameworks.

title: Bounding the Effect of HOD Assumptions on Small-Scale Clustering Constraints
summary: Small-scale galaxy clustering is expected to contain substantial cosmological information, but the extent to which this information constrains halo-based cosmologies independent of an assumed galaxy--halo connection remains unclear. We quantify this dependence using LRG-like mock galaxy catalogs built from 81 cosmologies in the {\tt \textsc{AbacusSummit}} suite. We analyze two-point correlation function multipoles on scales ranging from $5$--$80$ Mpc/$h$ and compare two limiting treatments, the \enquote{floor} and \enquote{ceiling}, of the standard five-parameter HOD model. In the conservative floor case, we impose only broad initial HOD bounds and profile over HOD parameters to determine the minimum constraining power available; we accomplish this with {\tt HODmin}, a two-stage global optimization algorithm written for minimizing $χ^2$ in HOD space. In the optimistic ceiling case, we assume the HOD parameters are known exactly. We find a significant difference between the floor and ceiling when comparing against the same Planck $Λ$CDM mock data vector with identical modeling assumptions: for the floor, $25\%$ of the discrete {\tt \textsc{AbacusSummit}} cosmologies tested are excluded at $3σ$, whereas for the ceiling, $\sim81\%$ are excluded. Many cosmologies agree well with data in the floor, and yet in the ceiling are excluded by multiple orders of magnitude in $χ^2$. We therefore observe the strength of small-scale clustering constraints depends heavily on the amount of prior HOD information assumed. We compare the sensitivity of this effect to various choices like scale cut, angle cut, multipole inclusion, mock phase, and mock HOD model. Our wide floor--ceiling bracket indicates that informative galaxy--halo priors are necessary for extracting strong small-scale clustering constraints.

AI.tldr: This study quantifies how assumptions about galaxy--halo connection impact cosmological constraints from small-scale galaxy clustering. Using mock data, they show that precise knowledge of Halo Occupation Distribution parameters greatly strengthens constraints, while broad uncertainties substantially weaken them. Robust cosmological inference thus demands informative galaxy--halo priors.
AI.motivation: To evaluate how the constraining power of small-scale galaxy clustering on halo-based cosmologies depends on assumptions about the galaxy--halo connection, particularly the Halo Occupation Distribution (HOD) parameters.
AI.method: Used Luminous Red Galaxy (LRG)-like mock catalogs from 81 cosmologies in the AbacusSummit simulation suite; analyzed two-point correlation function multipoles at 5--80 Mpc/h scales; employed two treatments of HOD modeling— a conservative "floor" with broad HOD parameter bounds optimized by the HODmin algorithm, and an optimistic "ceiling" assuming exact knowledge of HOD parameters; compared cosmology constraints under these two scenarios.
AI.result: Found a substantial difference in cosmology constraints between the floor and ceiling cases: the conservative floor excludes 25% of cosmologies at 3σ, while the optimistic ceiling excludes about 81%. Many cosmologies fit well under the floor but are strongly disfavored under the ceiling, indicating the strength of constraints depends strongly on prior HOD knowledge. This dependence was robust to variations in analysis choices such as scale and angle cuts, inclusion of multipoles, and mock realizations.
AI.conclusion: Small-scale galaxy clustering contains significant cosmological information, but extracting strong constraints requires informative priors on the galaxy--halo connection. Without such priors, constraints are considerably weaker, highlighting the critical role of galaxy--halo modeling assumptions in cosmological inference from clustering data.

title: Searching for cosmic vortices
summary: Our study focuses on the strong tidal disruption of a cold helium white dwarf passing a black hole. We model the white dwarf as a Bose-Fermi droplet and use quantum hydrodynamic equations to simulate the binary system's evolution. As the white dwarf passes through periastron, it loses a significant amount of mass. This mass falls onto the black hole and forms an accretion disc. Quantized vortices appear in the accretion disc, manifesting as strong electromagnetic radiation signals that exhibit characteristic flickering patterns changing on a timescale of a few seconds. Meanwhile, the white dwarf moves away from the black hole. As the white dwarf moves through space, vortices run along its surface. This elongates its geometry, causing it to rotate and emit gravitational waves.

AI.tldr: This study uses quantum hydrodynamics to model a cold helium white dwarf’s tidal disruption by a black hole, revealing quantized vortices that generate unique electromagnetic flickering and gravitational waves due to induced rotation and deformation.
AI.motivation: To understand the dynamics and observable signatures resulting from the strong tidal disruption of a cold helium white dwarf by a black hole, particularly focusing on quantum effects during the interaction.
AI.method: Modeling the white dwarf as a Bose-Fermi droplet and employing quantum hydrodynamic equations to simulate the evolution of the binary system during its periastron passage and subsequent interactions.
AI.result: The white dwarf loses significant mass forming an accretion disc around the black hole featuring quantized vortices that produce electromagnetic radiation with flickering patterns on timescales of seconds. Additionally, the white dwarf’s altered geometry and rotation from vortices on its surface lead to gravitational wave emission.
AI.conclusion: Quantum hydrodynamics provides critical insight into the tidal disruption of a helium white dwarf near a black hole, predicting distinctive electromagnetic and gravitational wave signals arising from vortex phenomena in the accretion disc and white dwarf surface.

title: Broadened Lensing Rings of Compact Boson Stars: Enhanced Imprint of Accretion Flow in Images and Visibilities
summary: In this work, we systematically study the gravitational lensing properties and observational signatures of compact boson stars. Unlike black holes, the photon effective potential of a compact boson star develops a nearly flat region, whose width increases with the compactness of the star. This flat structure significantly broadens the range of impact parameters that can produce large-angle deflections, leading to noticeably wider lensing rings of all orders. Photons constituting these rings traverse more complex paths, rendering the resulting images more sensitive to the spatial distribution of the accretion flow. Ray tracing results show that, compared to black hole models, the image topology and visibility amplitudes of compact boson stars exhibit a stronger dependence on the accretion flow structure. These results highlight qualitative differences in the observational properties of compact boson stars and black holes.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that compact boson stars produce wider lensing rings and more complex photon paths than black holes, resulting in observational signatures that are more sensitive to the surrounding accretion flow structure, highlighting key differences for astrophysical identification.
AI.motivation: To understand how compact boson stars differ from black holes in terms of gravitational lensing and their observational signatures.
AI.method: Systematic study of the gravitational lensing properties using photon effective potential analysis and ray tracing simulations of compact boson stars compared to black hole models.
AI.result: The compact boson stars have a nearly flat region in the photon effective potential which broadens the range of impact parameters producing large-angle deflections, resulting in wider lensing rings. The images show more complex photon paths, making image topology and visibility more sensitive to accretion flow structure than in black holes.
AI.conclusion: Compact boson stars exhibit qualitatively distinct gravitational lensing properties and observational signatures from black holes, particularly in image topology and sensitivity to the accretion flow, which can potentially be used to distinguish between these compact objects in observations.

title: SN 1006: A Cosmic Laboratory for Investigating Shock Acceleration Physics
summary: SN 1006 is a historical Type Ia supernova remnant that exhibits non-thermal emission ranging from radio to multi-TeV $γ$-rays. Most of this emission (particularly X-rays and $γ$-rays) is concentrated in polar caps aligned with the ambient magnetic field, which makes it an ideal laboratory for studying cosmic ray (CR) acceleration at different shock obliquities and the hadronic/leptonic nature of the $γ$-ray emission. We model SN 1006's morphology, multi-wavelength spectrum, and radial profile using a self-consistent multi-zone kinetic model of particle acceleration that accounts for: CR-driven shock modification, magnetic field amplification, drift in magnetic fluctuations, and temporal dynamics including adiabatic and synchrotron losses. Our model can reproduce both the observed spectral and spatial properties, with the exception of the radio profile that we argue requires 3D hydrodynamic effects to replicate. We find that quasi-parallel regions (where the shock normal aligns with the ambient magnetic field) exhibit very prominent CR acceleration ($\sim$20% efficiency), while quasi-perpendicular regions exhibit efficiencies below 1%, consistent with the results of kinetic simulations. We also find that electrons are responsible for the majority of the $γ$-ray emission from SN 1006 (i.e., it is a leptonic source), with the exception of the northwest region due to an encounter with a dense cloud.

AI.tldr: This study models SN 1006’s cosmic ray acceleration and gamma-ray emission, finding efficient acceleration in quasi-parallel shocks and a mainly leptonic gamma-ray source, except where dense cloud interaction induces hadronic emission.
AI.motivation: To understand cosmic ray acceleration mechanisms at varying shock obliquities and to clarify the hadronic versus leptonic origin of gamma-ray emission in the historical Type Ia supernova remnant SN 1006.
AI.method: A self-consistent multi-zone kinetic model of particle acceleration was employed, including cosmic ray-driven shock modification, magnetic field amplification, magnetic fluctuation drift, and temporal dynamics like adiabatic and synchrotron losses, to model the supernova remnant's morphology, spectrum, and radial profiles.
AI.result: The model successfully reproduces observed spectral and spatial features of SN 1006, except for the radio profile which likely requires 3D hydrodynamic modeling, confirms high acceleration efficiency in quasi-parallel shocks, low efficiency in quasi-perpendicular shocks, and establishes a predominately leptonic origin of gamma-rays except in interaction with a dense cloud.
AI.conclusion: SN 1006's non-thermal emission morphology and spectrum are primarily shaped by cosmic ray acceleration efficiencies dependent on shock obliquity, with quasi-parallel shocks showing high efficiency (~20%) and quasi-perpendicular shocks showing low efficiency (<1%). Electrons dominate the gamma-ray emission, except in the northwest where hadronic interactions occur due to dense cloud interaction.

title: Evidence for additional structure in the effective spin distribution hints at multiple formation pathways in GWTC-5.0
comment: Letter: 5 pages, 4 figures. Supplementary Material: 4 pages, 2 figures
summary: The distribution of the effective inspiral spin ($χ_\mathrm{eff}$) of the binary black holes detected by LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA can shed light on their formation pathways. We analyze the GWTC-5.0 dataset with two models-one flexible, one fully parametric-that jointly describe $χ_\mathrm{eff}$ and primary mass. We clarify that the previously-reported skewness in the $χ_\mathrm{eff}$ distribution is better understood as additional structure beyond a non-skewed Gaussian bulk centered at small $χ_\mathrm{eff}$. This additional structure extends to larger $|χ_\mathrm{eff}|$, a result previously reported using GWTC-4.0 data. We measure the asymmetry of the distribution of $χ_\mathrm{eff}$ outside the Gaussian bulk from the data. With both the parametric and the flexible analyses, we find tentative evidence for a mass-dependent excess of positive $χ_\mathrm{eff}$ over negative ones outside the Gaussian bulk. Only at $m_1 \in [46,65]\,M_\odot$ do the data require a negative $χ_\mathrm{eff}$ component outside the Gaussian bulk, with $23\text{:}1$ odds. If $χ_\mathrm{eff}$ outside the Gaussian bulk are produced by hierarchical mergers-as it has been suggested-then a fraction of those mergers may be produced in environments that can generate a surplus of binaries with positive $χ_\mathrm{eff}$, such as the disks of active galactic nuclei.

AI.tldr: The study analyzes LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA data on binary black hole spins, uncovering complex spin distribution features that suggest multiple formation pathways and environmental effects influencing spin orientations.
AI.motivation: To understand the formation pathways of binary black holes by studying the distribution of their effective inspiral spin ($χ_\mathrm{eff}$) detected by LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA.
AI.method: Analyzed the GWTC-5.0 dataset using two models (one flexible and one fully parametric) that jointly describe $χ_\mathrm{eff}$ and primary mass, focusing on characterizing the distribution of $χ_\mathrm{eff}$ beyond a Gaussian bulk.
AI.result: Found that the skewness previously reported in $χ_\mathrm{eff}$ distribution is better explained as additional structure extending beyond a non-skewed Gaussian centered at low $χ_\mathrm{eff}$. Tentative evidence shows a mass-dependent excess of positive $χ_\mathrm{eff}$ outside the Gaussian bulk, with significant negative $χ_\mathrm{eff}$ only in the mass range $46$ to $65 M_\odot$. This suggests hierarchical mergers and specific environments, like active galactic nuclei disks, might produce these features.
AI.conclusion: The $χ_\mathrm{eff}$ distribution reveals complex structure indicating multiple formation channels for binary black holes, including a mass-dependent imbalance in spin direction outside the Gaussian bulk likely linked to hierarchical mergers in specialized astrophysical environments.

title: Stellar mass loading drives dissipation and reacceleration in AGN jets: Explaining VLBI-Gaia offsets and constraining jet power
summary: Recent Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) and Gaia astrometry reveal systematic milliarcsecond-scale offsets between the radio and optical centroids of active galactic nuclei (AGN). These "radio-optical offsets" do not alter the standard opacity-driven interpretation of radio core shifts. Instead, they indicate that the optical emission centroid is frequently displaced downstream of the radio synchrotron optical depth $τ= 1$ surface, implying that additional dissipation and particle reacceleration occur beyond the opacity radio core within relativistic jets. We perform steady-state, axisymmetric relativistic magnetohydrodynamic (RMHD) simulations of AGN jets, including baryonic mass-load from stellar winds, varying jet kinetic power, and stellar core radius. Synthetic synchrotron emission maps in radio and optical bands are generated via a radiative transfer code, and centroid offsets are extracted for comparison with observations. Parsec-scale radio-optical offsets arise only for jet powers $L_{\rm j} \sim 10^{42.5} - 10^{44}\,\rm{erg}\,\rm{s}^{-1}$. In this regime, stellar winds trigger jet deceleration at intrinsic distances of a few $10^2-10^3\,\rm{pc}$, shifting the optical centroid downstream and producing offsets of $\sim 0.1 - 4\,\rm{mas}$ (a few tens of parsecs at $z=1$). Offsets depend on stellar distribution, viewing angle, and optical jet dominance, and vanish outside this power range. We reproduce the observed redshift evolution of offset incidence, linking it to the cosmic evolution of thermally pulsing asymptotic giant branch (TP-AGB) mass loss. Although stellar mass loading is unlikely to be the sole dissipation mechanism, its unavoidable presence in galactic nuclei makes it a natural baseline for energy dissipation. Radio-optical offsets therefore offer a constraint on AGN jet power and jet-host coupling, independent of traditional lobe-based methods.

AI.tldr: Simulations show that stellar winds cause parsec-scale radio-optical centroid offsets in AGN jets with specific power ranges, matching observations and linking offsets to stellar mass loss evolution; these offsets provide new constraints on jet power and jet-host coupling.
AI.motivation: To understand the origin of milliarcsecond-scale radio-optical centroid offsets in active galactic nuclei (AGN) revealed by VLBI and Gaia astrometry, which suggest additional dissipation beyond the radio core in relativistic jets.
AI.method: Performed steady-state, axisymmetric relativistic magnetohydrodynamic (RMHD) simulations of AGN jets with baryonic mass-load from stellar winds, varying jet kinetic power and stellar core radius; generated synthetic radio and optical synchrotron emission maps via radiative transfer to extract centroid offsets for observational comparison.
AI.result: Parsec-scale radio-optical offsets occur only for jet powers around 10^{42.5} to 10^{44} erg/s due to stellar wind-driven jet deceleration at hundreds to thousands of parsecs downstream, producing offsets of ~0.1 to 4 milliarcseconds that depend on stellar distribution, viewing angle, and jet dominance; results reproduce observed redshift evolution linked to TP-AGB star mass loss evolution.
AI.conclusion: Stellar mass loading in galactic nuclei causes jet deceleration and optical centroid displacement downstream of the radio core, naturally explaining observed radio-optical offsets. These offsets constrain AGN jet power and jet-host interactions independent of traditional radio lobe methods, although stellar mass loading is likely one of several dissipation mechanisms.

title: Time-dependent cosmic-ray escape from wind bubbles: hard spectra formation
summary: Overview: Wind-driven bubbles are dynamic systems that can accelerate cosmic rays, depending on their physical properties, up to very high energies. We investigate how a time-dependent description of the particle transport may impact the escaping cosmic-ray flux. Model: The wind bubble system is modeled as spherically symmetric. Cosmic rays are continuously injected at the position of the termination shock and propagate through advection and diffusion until the escape at the time-dependent position of the forward shock, which is treated as a free escape boundary. Methods: The one-dimensional spherical time-dependent transport equation is solved by transforming it into the corresponding set of stochastic differential equations, and integrated with a modified version of the open source cosmic-ray propagation framework CRPropa. Results: We find that, during the wind driven phase, the downstream escaping spectra from wind bubbles can be harder than $\sim E^{-2}$, the conventional expectation from diffusive shock acceleration. Depending on the turbulence model the initial energy spectrum can be significantly suppressed at lowest energies, which could be an observable feature to distinguish between different turbulence realizations. This effect could lead to an efficient confinement of low energy particles, potentially leading to observable implication in terms of multi-messenger radiation and cosmic-ray accumulated grammage within the bubble.

AI.tldr: This paper models cosmic-ray transport in wind-driven bubbles using time-dependent methods, finding harder-than-expected escaping spectra and turbulence-dependent suppression at low energies, which may yield observable multi-messenger signatures and insights into cosmic-ray confinement.
AI.motivation: To understand how time-dependent particle transport affects the escaping cosmic-ray flux from wind-driven bubbles, which are dynamic systems capable of accelerating cosmic rays to very high energies.
AI.method: Modeling the wind bubble system as spherically symmetric, with continuous cosmic ray injection at the termination shock; solving the one-dimensional spherical time-dependent transport equation via stochastic differential equations integrated with a modified CRPropa framework.
AI.result: During the wind-driven phase, escaping cosmic-ray spectra can be harder than the conventional $E^{-2}$ expectation. Low energy spectra can be significantly suppressed depending on turbulence models, leading to efficient confinement of low-energy particles and potential observable signatures in multi-messenger radiation and cosmic-ray accumulated grammage.
AI.conclusion: Time-dependent transport modeling reveals that cosmic-ray spectra escaping wind-driven bubbles can deviate substantially from conventional shock acceleration predictions, with turbulence-dependent features that could serve as observational diagnostics for turbulence and particle confinement in these environments.
